Model Fit

Classical Statistics. In classical statistics, a parametric model, such as linear regression, analysis of variance (ANOVA), a multilevel model, or a structural equation model, is selected and specified in a way that it best reflects the research questions. These models typically come with statistical assumptions, such as the normality of residuals in linear regression, that need to be assessed as part of the data analysis procedure. Parametric models are generally parsimonious and focus on a few theory-driven predictors and control variables. They are used to estimate model parameters (e.g., regression coefficients) and assess how much variance they explain (e.g.,

R-squared and the overall F-test).

In general, classical statistics tends to focus less on the performance of the model as a whole and more on the specific effects of predictors on the outcome variable, assuming the model overall has adequate fit.

Machine Learning. In contrast to classical statistics, ML models typically make few or no distributional assumptions about the data. Consequently, the global fit statistics and significance tests derived from statistical theory that are used to judge whether a classical model is adequate are generally not available. Statistical tests are still used in ML, for instance to compare the performance of two models or of a model against a baseline, but they do not serve to assess the adequacy of a single model in the way they do in classical statistics. Instead, the focus for assessing the quality of an ML model is using out-of-sample predictive performance, that is, how accurately it predicts new data that were not used for training. This evaluation is crucial because ML models are often flexible and can easily overfit the training data, meaning they become too good at modeling the training data such that they capture "noise" (e.g., random fluctuations) rather than or in addition to the underlying predictive patterns or "signal." To assess predictive performance on data unseen during training, the available data are typically split into separate subsets for training, validating, and testing models.

In a typical workflow, the data are therefore split into a training set used to fit a model, a validation set used for tuning and model selection evaluation, and, ideally, a test set held out for a final performance estimate (Hastie et al., 2009), as illustrated in Figure 3. The distinction between the terms validation and test set is not clear-cut, and not always consistently used. Throughout this article, we will adopt the description by Hastie et al. (2009) and use the term validation set for data used during model development to tune hyperparameters and to select among candidate models, and the term test set for data used only for the final estimate of predictive performance, never for fitting, tuning, or selecting the model. II. Model Evaluation

Training set Validation set Test set fit the model tune hyperparameters, select among models estimate final performance I. Model Development

Model flexibility is controlled by hyperparameters (e.g., the number of trees in RF), which are tuned by searching over candidate values and comparing predictive performance on unseen data. When the dataset is too small to be divided into sufficiently large training and test sets, resampling methods, particularly cross-validation (CV) in its various forms (e.g., k-fold, repeated, stratified, or nested CV), are commonly used to estimate predictive performance on unseen data.

The predictive performance itself is quantified using evaluation metrics, such as area under the curve for classification or mean squared error for regression. Throughout this process, it is important that researchers avoid data leakage (Kapoor & Narayanan, 2023), that is, information from the validation or test data inadvertently entering model training. For readers unfamiliar with these concepts, Web Supplement https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 describes the key aspects of a typical supervised ML workflow, including hyperparameter tuning, data splitting, CV and the risk of data leakage in more detail.

Identifying Informative Predictors

Classical Statistics. A central goal in psychological research is to explain the relationships between predictors and the outcome variable. In classical statistics, identifying predictors that are informative is often achieved through the significance test of each predictor or by means of model comparison. Thus, identifying informative predictors is often interlinked with fitting and selecting models, as indicated by the bidirectional arrow between model fit and identifying informative predictors in Figure 2.

Machine Learning.

In ML, the process of identifying informative features can differ from classical statistics. Some ML models automatically select informative features, for example, lasso regression, by shrinking coefficients to zero (Tibshirani, 1996). In most ML algorithms, the contribution of a feature is typically assessed using feature importance measures. Common examples are feature rankings based on permutation importance (Breiman, 2001a) or SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP; Lundberg & Lee, 2017). In addition, test-based and performance-based approaches aim to determine more formally whether a feature contributes to the ML model (e.g., Altmann et al., 2010; Guyon et al., 2002; Hapfelmeier & Ulm, 2013). Web Supplement https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 describes these importance measures and feature identification approaches in detail.

Interpreting Effects

Beyond the identification of informative predictors of the data analysis, we further distinguish interpreting effects as a separate stage in our framework. While identifying informative predictors describes which predictors are informative in explaining and predicting the outcome, interpretation informs researchers how these predictors are associated with the outcome.

Thus, interpretation refers to describing the direction (positive or negative), the shape (e.g., linear, curvilinear, or non-monotonic), and the strength (e.g., effect size) of the association between predictors and the outcome variable, as well as interactions among predictors in their effect on the outcome.

Classical Statistics.

Parametric methods in classical statistics provide effect size estimates (e.g., Cohen's d, Pearson's r, standardized regression coefficients) to interpret both magnitude and direction. Unlike p-values, which indicate statistical significance, effect sizes provide a measure for practical significance.

Parametric methods often assume linear relationships between predictors and the outcome variable. Consequently, a researcher's choice of model directly implies how results are interpreted (as illustrated by the link between model fit and interpretability in Figure 2). To capture non-linear relationships, researchers can incorporate polynomial or interaction terms, which need to be hypothesized and specified a priori rather than inferred from the data.

Although widely used in psychological research, effect sizes can be difficult to interpret.

Funder and Ozer (2019) caution against interpreting them using context-independent thresholds (e.g., Cohen, 2013) and recommend substantive interpretations based on relevant benchmarks. Machine Learning. Machine learning models are often referred to as black boxes because it is neither easy to see how the features are combined to generate model predictions, nor easy to ascertain the direction, shape, and strength of an effect. To shed light into the black box model, post-hoc supplementary interpretation techniques have been developed and are often referred to as explainable AI or interpretable ML (Gunning et al., 2019; Lavelle-Hill, Smith, Deininger, & Murayama, 2025; Molnar, 2025). Many of these techniques are model-agnostic, meaning that they can be applied to any ML model regardless of its characteristics. They can provide global interpretations, describing how features influence the model's predictions on average, or local interpretations, describing how features influence the prediction for an individual observation. Common examples are SHAP values and plots (Lundberg & Lee, 2017), Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME; Ribeiro et al., 2016), Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE; Goldstein et al., 2015) plots, Partial Dependence (PD; Friedman, 2001) plots, and Accumulated Local Effects (ALE; Apley & Zhu, 2020) plots. Some of these techniques can be used for both identification of informative features (stage 3; e.g., averaged absolute SHAP values) and their interpretation (stage 4; e.g., plotting SHAP values against feature values revealing shape and direction). Web Supplement https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 presents these techniques with visual examples. Further overviews are given by Henninger et al. (2025), Henninger and Strobl (2025),

Lavelle-Hill, Smith, Deininger, and Murayama (2025), and Molnar (2025).

Reporting the Analysis

As the fifth and final stage, researchers document and report their analysis. Inadequate reporting can lead to misunderstanding, making it difficult for researchers to understand, critically evaluate the quality of the analysis, and potentially replicate the study. In the context of ML, incomplete reporting can prevent reviewers and readers from identifying potential issues such as overfitting, underfitting, or data leakage.

Classical Statistics. When employing classical statistics in psychological research, researchers can follow established reporting practices such as the publication manual of the American Psychological Association (APA; American Psychological Association, 2020) or the JARS-Quant manual for reporting quantitative research (Appelbaum et al., 2018). The APA manual provides guidelines on what kind of information should be included in all manuscript sections for quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods research. For instance, researchers should include details on hypotheses and objectives, primary and secondary measures and covariates, study design, and the analytical strategy for inferential statistics. Moreover, the manual emphasizes the importance of reporting on the results of all inferential tests conducted, including p values and, when possible, the effect-size estimates and confidence intervals. Finally, in the discussion, a statement of support or non-support for the hypotheses should be included as well as an interpretation of the results. Luo et al. (2021) demonstrated, through the example of multilevel modeling, that reporting standards enhance the quality of reporting in various aspects.

Machine Learning. For ML applications, however, the APA publication manual does not (yet) provide specific reporting guidelines. Instead, individual researchers have published recommendations on best practices and pitfalls, such as a checklist for reporting ML analyses (Pargent et al., 2023) or an overview of questionable research practices like selective reporting of the best-performing model (Leech et al., 2024).

In research fields other than psychology, we find more reporting guidelines for ML applications, including the REFORMS recommendations for ML-based science (Kapoor et al., 2024). In health care, the TRIPOD+AI statement from Collins et al. (2024) guides the use of clinical prediction models developed using ML. Their checklist comprises items that address, for example, data preprocessing, defining candidate features, model development such as hyperparameter tuning, and model performance evaluation. They also emphasize reporting details on model updates that arise from model evaluation. Further examples come from digital health (Klement & El Emam, 2023), clinical research (Stevens et al., 2020), and environmental research (Zhu et al., 2023 (Zhu et al., , 2024)). Most of these guidelines, however, were developed for specific domains and may not transfer to psychology, where samples are smaller, constructs are often latent, and commonly explanation is a central research goal. First psychology-specific proposals have recently emerged (Min et al., 2026; Pargent et al., 2023), but they constitute individual recommendations rather than standards endorsed by the field. Thus, a consensus on psychology-specific reporting standards for ML is still largely absent.

The Present Study

In the present study, we map current practices in application and reporting of supervised ML in psychological research. Considering all five stages of the framework, we assess (1) how data are prepared before model fitting, (2) how models are tuned, evaluated, and selected, (3) how informative features are identified, (4) the extent to which interpretable ML techniques are used to answer the researchers' research question and gain insights into the ML model predictions, and ( 5) how researchers report their analysis.

Methods

We systematically reviewed psychological and psychiatric articles using supervised ML

Searching Articles

The database APA PsycInfo was searched through the Ovid research platform to identify empirical articles that mentioned RF, SVM, or NN in the title or in the abstract. We concentrated on these three widely applied supervised ML methods in psychological research (see Figure 1), given that other bagging and boosting algorithms were less commonly found and decision trees offer relatively straightforward interpretability.

We included articles published in 2022 as a representative sample amid the increasing application of ML methods in psychological research, and articles published between June 2024 and May 2025 to explore more recent ML applications.

These two samples enabled us to compare practices over time and identify potential developments.

During the identification phase, we excluded literature reviews or systematic reviews, scientific simulation studies, and articles that were not published in a psychological or psychiatric journalfoot_0.

The search history for the identification phase is available in Web Supplement https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933.

Piloting the Review Procedure

This review procedure was developed and piloted on articles published in 2021. They served as a training sample to develop and refine the review steps without using any articles from the test sample of 2022 and 2024/2025.

Developing the Codebook

First, articles from 2021 were utilized to define the characteristics of the stages of the framework outlined in Figure 2, which was then translated into a codebook. Each section of the codebook comprised items in both closed-and open-ended response formats. For closed-ended items, raters only indicated whether an item was met or not (e.g., "SHAP values were used or not used to describe the shape of an effect.", item from (4) interpreting effects). For open-ended items, they provided their own written responses or excerpts from the full texts (e.g., "Provide the exact section of the text where the preprocessing of features and data was described.", item from (1) data characteristics & preprocessing).

Rater Training

To familiarize the rater team (4 students, 2 experts) with the codebook, the raters independently coded the same randomly selected articles from the 2021 training sample and afterwards discussed their coding decisions to resolve discrepancies and to refine the codebook.

Two rounds of training were completed. To identify the items that needed refinement, we calculated the inter-rater reliability for every closed-ended item using the prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa (PABAK; Byrt et al., 1993), aiming for an at least substantial agreement 2 between the raters (PABAK > 0.61; Landis & Koch, 1977). Items that did not reach this criterion were reformulated into open-ended items and were coded by the experts whenever the raters reported the evaluation as challenging or unclear.

Since substantial agreement had been established during the training, each article from the test sample was subsequently coded by a single rater. The final version of the codebook used during the data extraction phase is available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933).

Abstract Screening Using an LLM

Each abstract was automatically screened by OpenAI's GPT-4o-mini model (OpenAI, 2024) to determine whether the article was further relevant or not (see Cai et al., 2025; Henninger et al., 2026). The prompt asked the LLM to evaluate the abstract based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria of the review, and an abstract was considered relevant if all criteria were fulfilled. The prompt was engineered using a training sample of 90 randomly selected articles published in 2021, and the model's performance was assessed by comparing its classifications (relevant/irrelevant) with those of a human rater (the first author) serving as a benchmark. To ensure robustness and generalizability of the criteria, we repeated this procedure with a new set of 30 randomly selected abstracts from the 2021 sample. In both assessments, the proportion of abstracts falsely classified as relevant (false positives: 0.267 and 0.233) was higher than the proportion of abstracts falsely classified as irrelevant (false negatives: 0.089 and 0.133), indicating a liberal inclusion strategy. We therefore considered the risk of missing relevant articles acceptable for a scoping review, which aims to map common practices rather than to identify 2 There are no clear criteria for determining when rater training is considered successful. Reported cut-off values range from kappa > 0.80 for include/exclude decisions (Pérez et al., 2020) to kappa > 0.41 for single items (Müller & Dragicevic, 2003). As we inspected many and more complex items in the codebook, we aimed for the lower bound of the substantial agreement benchmark (kappa > 0.61) proposed by Landis and Koch (1977).

every eligible article. Erroneously included articles were addressed during the data extraction of the full texts by the human rater team.

To account for the inherent variability of LLMs, we screened each abstract ten times and quantified the uncertainty of the responses to identify ambiguous cases (see also Kalai & Vempala, 2024). A response was considered consistent if it achieved more than 60% majority vote. Inconsistent cases were flagged as uncertain and manually reviewed by the first author (2022: n = 39; 2024/2025: n = 21 abstracts with at least one uncertain criterion).

Preparing Articles for Data Extraction

The screening pipeline was then applied to the abstracts of the identified articles from 2022 and 2024/2025 in order to identify those that met all criteria. Figure 4 summarizes the literature search strategy in a PRISMA flowchart of study selection, in which the Identification stage corresponds to the literature search described above, the Screening stage to the abstract screening using the LLM, and the subsequent stages to the raters' assessment of the full texts described below.

Coding Articles

Guided by the codebook, the rater team extracted data from the full texts of the articles that passed the abstract screening (Screening stage in Figure 4). The articles were coded in two batches, beginning with the sample from 2022 and followed by the sample from 2024/2025. The raters were directed to read the articles as a typical reader would: To answer an item, they relied on the main text and consulted supplementary materials only when the article explicitly referred to them.

Analyzing Articles

To prepare the coded data for analysis, the first author, where necessary together with the senior author, examined the full texts to review any unclear cases reported by the raters. Cases that remained unresolved were documented as unclear or not mentioned.

Closed-ended items were summarized as proportions of studies meeting each item.

Transparency and Openness

We report how we determined our sample (i.e., the search strategy and eligibility criteria), all article exclusions, and all coded measures in the codebook. The review was preregistered on January 28, 2025 (https://osf.io/6ve4f/), and all deviations from the preregistration are documented in Web Supplement E. The web supplements, including the coded data, analysis code, codebook (including a documentation of all item-specific changes), rater training materials, screening materials, and a list of all reviewed articles are available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933). Data were analyzed using R 4.5.3 (R Core Team, 2025); open-ended items were analyzed using MAXQDA 2022 (VERBI Software, 2021).

Apart from its documented use in abstract screening and category building (see above), we used generative artificial intelligence (AI; Claude; Anthropic, 2026) to improve the language and structure of the manuscript, to help write R code (e.g., for data processing and figures), and to aid the search for relevant literature. We checked and revised all AI-generated content and take full responsibility for the final manuscript.

Results

We structure the results presentation using the first four stages of our framework; the fifth stage, reporting, is assessed throughout: for each stage, the raters additionally judged how clearly and comprehensibly the analysis was reported (the ratings for all four stages are reported in https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.241629331 in Web Supplement H).

After the raters coded the full text of the selected 271 articles, we further excluded 39 articles that did not meet our inclusion criteria based on the information provided in the articles, resulting in a final sample of 232 articles (152 articles were published in 2022 and 80 articles were published between June 2024 and May 2025foot_2 ). Unless stated otherwise, the percentages we report refer to the proportion of reviewed articles in the respective time period. Where the unit of analysis is not the article, for example, studies, datasets, or models within an article, we state this explicitly.

Data Characteristics and Preprocessing

Data Dimensionality

Given that ML is capable of analyzing high-dimensional data, we expected that researchers in psychology might increasingly apply ML to these datasets where classical statistics falls short. these low-dimensional data (2022: n = 50 datasets from 37 studies; 2024/2025: n = 23 datasets from 19 studies; see https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.241629331 in Web Supplement I) revealed that most researchers justified their ML models by emphasizing practical advantages of ML or good performance results from previous studies or analyses. 4 The different categories were retrieved from the Journal Citation Reports Data from the Web of Science Core Collection (Clarivate, 2025). The category "Neuroscience" was built manually based on journals that have "Neuro" in their name (e.g., Frontiers in Human Neuroscience). In nine journals where the database listed multiple psychological categories, the first author manually assigned the category that best matched the journal's primary scope.

For What Kind of Datasets Do Researchers Use Machine Learning?

Data Types and Preprocessing

Background information, such as the individuals' demographic data or clinical diagnoses, was present in the majority of datasets, followed by questionnaire data (mostly standardized, named inventories, but also formal clinician-led interviews and unspecified questionnaires) and imaging data (see https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.241629331 in Web Supplement J). In both time periods, background information most often occurred alongside at least one other data type, while data from genes, sensors, EEG, and other sources were relatively rare.

Data preprocessing was reported in many cases (2022: n = 121, 79.61%; 2024/2025: n = 62, 77.5%), most commonly involving the creation of new features or indices from the raw data (e.g., calculating scores from questionnaire items; see Table 1). Nearly as common were data-specific processing protocols, such as standard pipelines for preparing neuroimaging data from various modalities (e.g., fMRI, EEG), as well as data cleaning (e.g., outlier detection and processing) and missing data imputation. Whether such preprocessing steps were carried out before or after the data were split, and thus whether information from the test data could have leaked into model training, was rarely reported (we return to this issue in the Discussion). Data dimensionality reduction methods (e.g., principal component analysis) were also employed in preparation for the forthcoming application of ML. These approaches were similarly common in both time periods.

Defining Candidate Features

The process of defining candidate features (2022: n = 67, 44.08%; 2024/2025: n = 34, 42.5%) prior to the main analysis was often based on theory or expert knowledge. Besides, researchers also frequently included features following a data-driven assessment, which involved selecting features based on univariate statistical tests, such as t-tests, ANOVA, chi-squared tests, or correlation analyses. For example, H. Yan et al. (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933)* reported recognizing abnormal values in voxel data using t-tests and inputting the resulting feature values into an SVM. Other researchers employed multivariate, model-based feature selection techniques that make use of forward or backward selection algorithms or regularization methods (e.g., lasso regression or elastic net). All these approaches have in common that researchers consider which candidate features to provide to the main ML model(s) in order to reduce the overall number of features to a set of informative features that are relevant for the model's outcome. Model Fit

Models and Implementation

In general, we observed that, in addition to RF, SVM, and NN, generalized linear models (e.g., logistic regression), boosting methods, and regularized regression techniques (e.g., lasso regression) frequently served as baseline or comparison models (see https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.241629331 in Web Supplement K). Regarding implementation, R was the most commonly used programming language in 2022, followed by Python and then MATLAB, whereas Python was the most common programming language in 2024/2025 (see Table 4). Notably, the programming language remained unclear or unmentioned in almost a third of the articles from 2022 but in none of the articles from 2024/2025.

Hyperparameter Tuning

From our focal models, RF, SVM, and NN, the hyperparameters of at least one model were tuned in 44.74% of the articles in 2022 and 57.5% of the articles in 2024/2025. This result indicates, first, a substantial proportion of https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 who did not perform any tuning or optimization of their models, and second, an increase in the proportion of researchers who conducted tuning in 2024/2025 compared to 2022. If hyperparameter tuning was performed, it was mostly executed using a grid search approach. Furthermore, CV was utilized for tuning in various forms, such as standard k-fold CV or nested CV. We also observed articles in which tuning was performed, but the details of the tuning process were not provided, such as which hyperparameters were tuned, which values were considered, and which tuning strategy was used (e.g., grid search, random search, or model-specific automated tuning). In a few cases, researchers provided such superficial reporting that it became difficult to determine whether tuning was performed at all, for example, when a model was described merely as "optimized."

Evaluation Strategies

In both time periods, performance evaluation was conducted in the majority of articles (2022: n = 148, 97.37%; 2024/2025: n = 77, 96.25%). Table 2 summarizes the evaluation strategies used. In both time periods, most researchers evaluated the models' predictive performance based on CV, such as k-fold or leave-one-out CV (see Table 3). Fewer researchers drew on other CV techniques, such as repeated or nested CV. As would be expected, nested CV was mostly applied to comparatively small datasets in both time periods (2022: 30 datasets from 13 articles with Mdn = 192.5 observations per dataset, IQR = 93-380, range = 41-5863; 2024/2025: 9 datasets from 8 articles with Mdn = 253 observations per dataset, IQR = 56-551, range = 20-12818), with only a few notably larger datasets in each period (2022: n = 5863; 2024/2025: n = 6109, 12818). Besides CV, splitting the data into training and validation sets or evaluating on an independent test set was less common, with an increase in recent articles from 2024/2025. Moreover, some researchers also combined both strategies, such as splitting data and performing CV on the training set and evaluating the final model on a test set, in particular in 2024/2025. By "splitting" data, we do not necessarily refer to randomly partitioning just a single dataset. Researchers have also worked with multiple datasets, where one dataset was used for training and another independent test set with samples from a different cohort or time period was used for testing. In some instances, researchers assessed the models' performance and reported some evaluation metrics (an overview of the metrics used can be found in https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.241629332 in Web Supplement K) but did not specify a particular evaluation strategy, making it challenging to understand how the evaluation was carried out. Others documented the evaluation strategy but did not report any evaluation metrics, which made it difficult to assess the models' performance. Note. These proportions are based on the articles that evaluated the performance of at least one machine learning model (2022: n = 148, 97.37%; 2024/2025: n = 77, 96.25%). Articles that evaluated only the out-of-bag error of an RF, a performance estimate specific to RFs (2022: n = 3; 2024/2025: n = 2), and articles that reported an evaluation outcome but did not mention the evaluation strategy were assigned to the category in which researchers neither used cross-validation nor data splitting.

Evaluation Metrics

The models' predictive performance was commonly evaluated using metrics such as (balanced) accuracy (number of correct predictions divided by the total number of predictions), area under the ROC curve, sensitivity, and specificity for classification tasks, and 𝑅 2 and (root) mean squared error for regression tasks (see https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.241629332 in Web Supplement K). The evaluation measures were also often used to compare different models 6 to determine which model performed 6 We use the term "different models" broadly, as the reviewed articles compared models on several levels. Some compared different model types, that is, different learning algorithms applied to the same data (e.g., an RF against an NN). Others compared multiple specifications of the same model type, for example, the same algorithm trained on different sets of features, predicting different outcomes, or fitted with different hyperparameter configurations. We counted all of these as comparisons between models.

best for a specific task. Some researchers additionally tested the statistical significance of the evaluation metrics against a null distribution, for example, by using permutation testing. Identifying Informative Variables

Figure 6 shows that in most articles, researchers did identify informative variables using different strategies for variable selection, with even higher proportions in more recent articles from 2024 and 2025. The figure is organized by thematic groupings -variable importance ranking, test-based approaches, and other approaches -each of which is discussed in the

following subsections.

Variable Importance Ranking

Most researchers calculated variable importance measures for each feature, which quantify the importance of a feature in a model. The features were subsequently ranked based on these importance scores, and the top features were then marked as informative or important contributors to the model's outcome. The choice of the number of "top most important" features (e.g., 5 or 10) was arbitrary, often remained unjustified, followed heuristics, and varied across studies. The utilized importance measures also varied among the studies.

In both time periods, the most commonly used importance measures were the permutation importance (i.e., the decrease in prediction accuracy when a feature's values are permuted or shuffled; Breiman, 2001a) or the refitting importance (i.e., the decrease in prediction accuracy when a feature is removed and the model is subsequently refitted), followed by rankings based on mean absolute SHAP values or combinations of those. Further, rankings were compared based on different models or samples (see, e.g., https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933)*. In a substantial proportion of the articles reviewed, a ranking was reported, but the importance measure was not specified or mentioned.

Test-Based Approaches

Besides considering variable importance rankings, some researchers also conducted statistical tests to determine the significance of feature importance, for example, by applying already existing packages and algorithms that perform permutation testing, such as the Boruta method (Kursa & Rudnicki, 2010), the permutation method (Altmann et al., 2010), or by implementing custom, self-written, permutation testing procedures. Some of the descriptions of these procedures remained vague, whereas others provided a more detailed explanation, such as

Juen et al. (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933)* stating: "Notably, this approach introduces a novel metric known as 'variable importance' (VI) for each predictor. [. . . ] To ascertain the statistical significance of these VI measurements, the random forest analyses were repeated 5000 times using shuffled outcome measures. Subsequently, random chance importance measures and standard deviations were calculated for each predictor. A Z-test with Bonferroni correction was then applied to determine the likelihood of observing high VI values due to chance." (p. 4) One article from 2022 conducted variable selection using one-way ANOVA post-hoc tests to compare the importance scores across three differently trained classification models (Doi et al., 2022)*.

Other Approaches

Other approaches to identify informative variables included performance-based selections, where, for example, different feature sets were used as input into a model and the resulting performance was compared. Thus, features achieving high average accuracies among all models stood out as "critical indicators" and served as "justifiable discriminative attributes" for an

Interpreting Effects

In the fourth stage of our framework, we focus on whether and how researchers interpreted the nature of the relationship between the features and the outcome of an ML model. While variable importance rankings describe which features drive the model, interpretations of these rankings remain limited. Interpretation techniques provide insights into how features are related to the model's outcome, such as the strength and shape of an effect, both describing its direction, as well as the interactions between featuresfoot_3.

Figure 7 summarizes our findings regarding the interpretation of ML results. In general, most researchers did not interpret the relationship between features and the model's outcome at all. This was observable in both time periods, but a higher proportion of articles did interpret their results in 2024/2025. When results were interpreted, researchers most commonly assessed the strength of an effect, followed by the shape of the effect and any interactions. Regarding strength, researchers frequently calculated the bivariate linear correlations between the features and the outcome, or they drew on the interpretable weights of a model. These weights can be derived from conducting post-hoc statistical linear models or from ML models, such as weights from support vector regression. Rarely, researchers interpreted an effect size in terms of how much the predicted outcome changes over different values of a feature, for example, by calculating the difference in predicted probabilities between two values of a feature. As one example, Zhang et al.

(https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933)* utilized partial dependence measures, illustrating "that the risk [of positive post-traumatic stress disorder] does not change by age between 5 and 16 while there is a 50% increase around age 16, leaping from .096 CI [.0871, .106] to .157 CI [.148, .166]." Researchers also interpreted the shape and direction of an effect by means of visualization techniques, primarily partial dependence plots in 2022, and SHAP visualizations in both time periods -however, SHAP values seem to have gained prominence over time. Interaction effects were more frequently analyzed in 2024/2025, often utilizing additional statistical linear modeling and SHAP. Other interpretation approaches were employed less frequently: saliency maps, descriptive statistics, or ML-based approaches, such as interpreting a decision tree or including regularization methods. The results were frequently discussed in relation to the importance of the features and were also connected to previous literature and theories.

Associational language (e.g., "the predictor is associated with the outcome") was predominantly used in these discussions, while quasi-causal language (e.g., "the predictor affects the outcome") was less common (see Table 5 for more details).

Discussion

In this scoping review, we examined how researchers in psychology apply and report supervised ML across two time periods. In the following, we critically discuss these findings along the five stages of our data analysis framework and derive explicit recommendations for applied researchers for each stage.

Data Characteristics and Preprocessing

Contrary to our assumption, ML was mostly applied to low-dimensional data. This is surprising, as a key advantage of ML is handling high-dimensional data, including settings in None None None None Corr. Interp. Wts Eff. which the number of features exceeds the number of observations (p > n). In many low-dimensional settings in which we observed ML use, classical statistical methods would likely be sufficient to analyze the data. However, applying ML to this type of data can be a reasonable choice when researchers aim at detecting previously unknown non-linear relationships and interactions, and this rationale was among the most commonly stated for applying ML. However, there may also be situations where ML models can show worse behavior compared to more constrained models, for instance under conditions typical for psychological data, such as measurement error or noisy data (Jacobucci & Grimm, 2020; McNamara et al., 2022; Speck et al., 2026).

In a number of articles, candidate features were defined a priori by means of univariate statistical screening, such as t-tests or correlation-based filters, and only the features that passed this screening were handed over to the ML model. Because these methods assess each feature univariately and in part assume a linear association with the outcome, a feature might be inappropriately discarded, potentially missing out on important non-linear relationships or interaction effects. When the goal is capturing non-linearity and interactions, screening by means of linear and univariate statistics is methodologically inconsistent and undermines the key advantage of using ML.

Data leakage can occur during preprocessing, when information from the validation or test data is inadvertently used during training and thereby undermines the assessment of generalizability (Dwyer et al., 2018). Based on the information provided in the reviewed articles, we were often unable to determine whether information from the test data could have leaked into model training. A concrete example is missing data imputation, where it was rarely stated whether imputation was performed before or after the data were split. Clear statements such as "missing data were imputed on the training set and the testing set independently to avoid data leakage" (Stafford et al., 2022)* were the exception rather than the rule. This may make it harder for readers and reviewers to judge the quality of the performance evaluation, and may also undermine transparency, replicability, and reproducibility.

Recommendations

We recommend that researchers motivate their use of ML and state what they expect to learn from it. For readers, it is informative whether ML was chosen, for example, because the number of features is large relative to, or even exceeds, the number of observations. Further, ML may be used because complex non-linear relationships and interactions are expected. When this is the motivation, researchers should refrain from univariate linear pre-filtering. Instead, when theory or expert knowledge is available, it can be used to define candidate features, which can benefit the reliability and generalizability of the results (Elhai & Montag, 2020). When such knowledge is lacking, the full feature space can be handed over to an ML model, whose selection mechanisms are compatible with non-linear associations. Finally, because preprocessing steps such as imputation, scaling, or feature selection can cause data leakage, researchers should make sure, and state explicitly, that these steps are carried out after the data have been split, and, when CV is used, repeated within each fold on the training part of that fold only. Implementing this correctly is easiest with established ML frameworks, which bundle preprocessing and model into a single pipeline that is resampled as a whole, such as mlr3 for R users (Lang et al., 2019) or scikit-learn for Python users (Buitinck et al., 2013; Pedregosa et al., 2011).

Model Fit

Cross-validation is a well-established method for assessing predictive performance and helping to detect overfitting (Koul et al., 2018; Pargent et al., 2023). It is encouraging that it has now become standard practice for ML model evaluation in psychological research, in particular when comparing ML work from 2022 to more recent work from 2024/2025. In the more recent time period, we also more frequently observed that CV on the training data was combined with an additional evaluation on a previously split test set. This is one possible strategy, but repeated or nested CV can serve the same purpose of separating the training (including parameter tuning and model selection) from the final evaluation.

Hyperparameter tuning, in contrast, was often absent or unreported, and we see two possible explanations. First, it may be a reporting issue. Machine learning remains difficult to publish in classical psychology journals, and methodological details such as tuning procedures may be shortened or removed during revisions to keep an article accessible to reviewers and readers. Second, it may be a methodological issue, meaning that some researchers did not tune their models at all. Not tuning could also reflect a practical trade-off, for example when computational resources are focused on producing explanations because the primary interest lies in interpretation rather than maximal predictive performance. Ideally, however, the interpreted model is also the best-performing one. Hyperparameters control model flexibility and can substantially affect predictive performance and liability to overfitting, especially in high-dimensional settings (A Ilemobayo et al., 2024; Bischl et al., 2023), but not to the same degree across methods. Support Vector Machines and NN are highly sensitive to their hyperparameters, whereas RFs are comparatively robust and often perform reasonably well with default settings, although tuning can still improve their performance (Probst, Wright, et al., 2019; Probst, Boulesteix, et al., 2019). Where tuning is performed, models should not be tuned and evaluated on the same data. If the best-performing model variant is selected on the same data on which its performance is then reported, that performance estimate is likely optimistically biased (Cawley & Talbot, 2010).

Nested CV, however, was applied only rarely, and mostly to comparatively small datasets. This pattern is expected: when samples are small, setting aside a separate validation set for tuning would leave very little data for evaluation, so nesting the tuning inside the resampling is a good strategy on limited samples.

Recommendations

We recommend that researchers report their analysis pipeline thoroughly and comprehensively, including what data were used for data splitting, imputation and other preprocessing steps, tuning, and evaluation. Whether and how hyperparameters were tuned should be stated explicitly, including the rationale when models were deliberately not tuned but run with the default settings. When models are tuned, tuning and performance evaluation need to be separated, for instance by tuning with CV on the training data and evaluating on a separate test set or by nested CV (see Web Supplement https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933 for an applied example using a nested and stratified assessment approach, see Opoku Asare et al., 2021). The article should make clear which of these strategies was used. When journal constraints limit the level of methodological detail in the main text, these details should be moved to supplementary materials, preregistrations, or updates to preregistrations, rather than omitted.

Identifying Informative Variables

For most researchers, variable importance rankings served as the endpoint of the analysis.

Features were ranked by an importance measure, and a number of top-ranked features were declared informative or important. Even though interpreting variable importance is a valuable step in shedding light on the ML model, we see two potential issues with the current practices in psychology. First, rankings depend on the importance measure employed, yet in many articles the specific measure was not clearly stated. Second, the number of top features considered important followed heuristics and as such was an arbitrary number. This analytic flexibility may open the door for cherry-picking, as researchers can report the features that most closely match their expectations (Leech et al., 2024).

When researchers used multiple importance measures, the resulting rankings can diverge. This situation is not unique to ML: In classical statistics, information criteria such as the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria can also favor different models because they value model parsimony differently. Similarly, SHAP values and different types of permutation importance (e.g., conditional versus unconditional importance) are conceptually distinct measures and may lead to different importance rankings without necessarily implying a methodological inconsistency. For example, SHAP values quantify how much a feature contributes to the individual predictions, aggregated across observations, whereas permutation importance quantifies how much predictive performance drops when a feature is randomly shuffled. Conditional and unconditional permutation importance differ further in how they attribute importance among correlated features (Strobl et al., 2008). Researchers should transparently report when variable importance rankings differ for different importance measures, and discuss whether this implies a potential limitation of the findings or not. In a similar vein, test-based approaches for identifying informative features may appear to be a principled alternative to arbitrary cutoffs, but also need to be described in detail so readers can judge their validity. Furthermore, a recent simulation study indicates that the majority of these tests have poor statistical properties (Rothacher & Strobl, 2023) and necessitate further evaluation before they should be applied in ML practice.

Recommendations

We recommend that researchers always explicitly name the importance measure they used and describe how it was computed. The measure and the rule for selecting informative features should be specified before the analysis, ideally as part of a preregistration of the entire analysis pipeline (for a template, see Hofman et al., 2023; for an example of a preregistered ML study, see Glunz et al., 2026). When feasible, we encourage computing multiple importance measures, comparing the resulting rankings, and discussing potential divergence in light of what the measures are designed to capture (e.g., https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933)*. Where rankings are compared across different models rather than across measures, this is only informative when the models achieve similar predictive performance, that is, when they form a so-called Rashomon set (Dong & Rudin, 2020; Lavelle-Hill et al., 2021). Regarding test-based approaches, we recommend that researchers correct for multiple testing, and account for uncertainty introduced by feature selection prior to the ML application. The latter can be achieved, for example, by using independent data for feature selection and inference (e.g., splitting the data), by utilizing feature selection within resampling (e.g., using [nested] CV), or where available, by using post-selection inference methods (e.g., for the lasso, see Lee et al., 2016). In general, importance analyses deserve the same reporting rigor as any other main result, because in most of the reviewed articles, the substantive conclusions rested on them.

Interpreting Effects

Most researchers ended their analysis having answered which features matter and did not examine how the features are related to the outcome. The strength, shape, and direction of effects, as well as interactions, were only rarely interpreted, even though the assessment of non-linearities and interactions is a key advantage of ML analyses and could inform future studies and potentially theories (Van Lissa, 2023). Against this background, it is interesting that SHAP (Lundberg & Lee, 2017) appeared to gain prominence in the more recent time period, which speaks to the growing popularity and accessibility of interpretable ML techniques (for overviews, see Lavelle-Hill, Smith, Deininger, & Murayama, 2025; Molnar, 2025).

We were surprised, however, to find a substantial proportion of researchers who interpreted effects based on bivariate correlations or post-hoc parametric linear models after applying ML to the data. This mirrors the univariate linear pre-filtering discussed above, only at the other end of the analysis: When linear models are used to finally interpret the results, non-linear patterns and interactions are masked, and the advantage that motivated the use of ML in the first place is forgone at the final step of the analysis.

Recommendations

We recommend that researchers who are interested in how features relate to the outcome make use of existing interpretable ML techniques, such as PD, ICE, and ALE plots or SHAP values. An introduction to these techniques with illustrations is provided in Web Supplement https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933. These techniques allow researchers to examine the strength, shape, and direction of effects, as well as interactions, without imposing linearity on the fitted model (Henninger & Strobl, 2025; Molnar, 2023; for an application, see Guo et al., 2025). When researchers deliberately use post-hoc linear models to interpret their results, they should state the rationale explicitly and acknowledge that non-linear patterns captured by the ML model may not be represented in the interpretation. When several interpretation techniques are applied, all results should be presented and discussed. The same caution applies to interpreting several models side by side, which, as noted above, presupposes that they are similarly accurate.

Reporting

Transparent reporting is relevant across all previous stages, and its quality varied considerably between articles. Our findings suggest that reporting improved from 2022 to 2024/2025, most clearly for model fitting and evaluation, which is a positive development.

Detailed results on this topic are provided in Web Supplement https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24162933. Nonetheless, key information was often missing or unclear, such as which hyperparameters were tuned, how CV was set up, or in which order preprocessing and data splitting were performed, the latter being critical for ruling out data leakage. In several cases, the raters could not determine whether an analysis step was carried out at all. We attribute part of this heterogeneity to the absence of established ML reporting standards in psychology during the time periods we examined. Our findings converge with Min et al. (2026), who examined supervised ML applications across 11 psychology journals and likewise found a pronounced lack of consistency in the reporting of key methodological information.

Moreover, best practices partly depend on the data and the research question at hand, which makes developing general standards a difficult task.

Cherry-picking is not limited to the selection of top features. More generally, researchers can try many models, seeds, data splits, evaluation metrics, and importance measures and report only the most favorable combination (Leech et al., 2024). That such choices are consequential is not merely a theoretical concern: Coles et al. (2025) showed that results depend substantially on the methodological decisions made along the analysis pipeline. Preregistration of ML workflows, which we observed only rarely (2022: n = 4, 2.63%; 2024/2025: n = 10, 12.5%), is a natural countermeasure to address this flexibility.

Recommendations

Until field-wide standards exist, we recommend that researchers follow the recently proposed psychology-specific checklist by Min et al. (2026), domain-specific guidelines such as the TRIPOD+AI checklist from Collins et al. (2024), or best-practice guidance, such as the tutorial by Pargent et al. (2023). The checklist by Min et al. (2026) is tailored to psychological research questions and manuscript structure and therefore requires less adaptation. It does not, however, address data leakage with regard to the reporting of preprocessing data, which we identified above as a concern that readers and reviewers were frequently unable to rule out. We therefore see the leakage-related topics discussed in the previous sections as a necessary extension of such checklists (see also Lavelle-Hill, 2026). We further recommend specifying the entire analysis pipeline prospectively, ideally in a preregistration (e.g., Hofman et al., 2023) or as a registered report (Jankowsky et al., 2026). As a guiding principle, an article should describe the analysis in enough detail that an independent researcher could reconstruct the entire pipeline from the raw data to the reported results. Where the data themselves cannot be shared, publishing the analysis code openly is usually still possible and goes a long way toward this goal.

Limitations

Our review has several limitations. First, we searched a single database, APA PsycInfo, and limited the search to psychological and psychiatric journals. We may have missed psychological articles that intersect with other disciplines and were not captured in APA PsycInfo.

Second, as preregistered, our search was restricted to articles mentioning RF, SVM, or NN in the title or abstract. Studies referring to their methods only with broader terms such as "machine learning" or "artificial intelligence" were therefore not captured, and terminology is changing so rapidly that we may have missed out on potential articles to be reviewed. Since our conclusions concern common analytical practices and are conceptual rather than focused on specific numbers or proportions, as would be the case in a meta-analysis, we expect that including such studies would not meaningfully alter our conclusions, takeaways, and importantly the recommendations derived from the review results. Third, despite the liberal inclusion strategy of the LLM-based abstract screening, some eligible articles were potentially excluded erroneously. Fourth, the reporting quality of the reviewed articles limited what we could code. We captured what researchers reported, not what they actually did, and unclear descriptions of, for example, tuning or evaluation strategies introduced uncertainty into the coding. Fifth, comparisons between the two time periods are descriptive. The two samples differ in size and database coverage, so temporal trends should be interpreted with caution.

Outlook

We see two methodological directions for future developments. As shown above, most of the reviewed articles analyzed data typical for psychology, which usually come with comparatively small samples. In addition to the measurement error and noise discussed above, small sample sizes have been shown to affect the performance of ML methods (Jacobucci & Grimm, 2020; Lavelle-Hill, Smith, & Murayama, 2025; McNamara et al., 2022; Speck et al., 2026). This raises the question of whether the available sample is large enough to train, tune, and evaluate an ML model, or to set aside a hold-out set, which is largely unsolved and makes sample size planning the first important direction for future research that we would like to point out. Traditional power analysis does not translate to ML, because its core concepts of effect size and statistical power have no direct equivalents there. Recent simulation-based approaches provide first guidance for clinical prediction models (Shamsutdinova et al., 2026), but comparable methods addressed to psychological audiences are not yet available. The second direction is the development of psychology-specific reporting standards for ML. The checklist by Min et al. (2026) constitutes an important first step in this direction. What is still missing is the transition from individual proposals to standards that are informed by a systematic look at existing guidelines from other fields and accepted by the field as a whole, ideally developed under the umbrella of the APA, for example as an extension of the JARS-Quant reporting standards (Appelbaum et al., 2018).

These directions translate into implications for different actors in the field. Editors and reviewers could explicitly encourage the supplementary reporting of ML methodology recommended above and reconsider how ML manuscripts are assigned and reviewed. Reviewers and readers need accessible tools, such as checklists, to judge the quality of ML applications without being ML experts themselves. Finally, lecturers and teachers shape the long-term development of the field. Machine learning is not yet part of the standard curriculum in psychology programs, and integrating it, including the programming languages in which ML is increasingly implemented, such as Python, would prepare the next generation of researchers and reviewers to apply and judge these methods. Ultimately, the ability to judge whether an ML application is rigorous, reliable, and replicable would then no longer rest on the individual expertise of a few methodologically trained readers but on standards, training, and reviewing practices that the field builds collectively.

In the following, we describe each step of the literature review: the literature search, the automated screening of abstracts using a large language model (LLM; GPT-4o-mini), the coding of the included articles by trained raters, and the analysis of the coded data. The literature review was preregistered on January 28, 2025. The preregistration is available on the Open Science Framework (OSF); all deviations from the original protocol are documented in Web Supplement E.

Figure5illustrates the dimensionality of the datasets used in the reviewed articles, with the left side representing 125 articles from 2022 and the right side representing 68 articles from 2024/2025, each consisting of one or multiple datasets. In some cases, information regarding the number of features in the dataset was unclear or missing (2022: n = 27, 17.76%; 2024/2025: n = 12, 15%). In general, and contrary to our assumption, most articles used low-dimensional data, characterized by a relatively small number of observations (n) and an even smaller number of features (p). In most articles, an observation typically referred to a person within a dataset, while in other articles, an observation represented an image, an experimental trial of an individual, or, in one case, operational records from a bus. Regarding features, most articles used tabular data, in which a feature typically referred to a property of an observation (e.g., an individual's background information or clinical diagnosis). However, in other articles, a feature represented a pixel or a voxel from imaging data, a single word from a text, or functional connectivity measures from fMRI or EEG. Only a few articles used ML on datasets with high-dimensional settings. This finding remained consistent across both time periods. Our data showed no recognizable clustering pattern across psychological fields 4 in either time period (for a more detailed look into the low-dimensional settings see FigureI1in Web Supplement I). These findings raise the question whether factors other than high dimensionality motivated researchers to use ML. Researchers provided a justification for ML use in 50.66% of the articles from 2022 and 65% of the articles from 2024/2025. In those cases, researchers commonly stated concrete practical advantages of ML, such as RF being "unrestricted by assumptions and well suited to handle a large number of predictors [. . . ] especially useful for identifying patterns in large and complicated datasets" (Ganai et al., 2024)* 5 or it "allows [. . . ] to model potential interactions and non-linearity among features in predicting the outcome" (Marengo et al., 2022)*. However, in some cases, the justification focused rather on performance, noting, for example, that "based on the predictive performances of previous depression-related mental health [. . . ] predictions, four ML techniques were developed" (Zhou et al., 2022)*. Some articles mentioned selecting so-called "state-of-the-art" models, a term that describes a top-performing model for a specific task at a specific time (Paul et al., 2022; Rastpour & McGregor, 2022)*. Other researchers emphasized that specific ML models were already commonly used in their field, such as SVMs, which "are widely used in biomedical research to diagnose severe mental illnesses" (He et al., 2022)*. (2024)*, a set of features (speech features only) yielded "high predictive accuracy for fatigue detection," with the observation that "adding more features only marginally improved the model performance, suggesting that a subset of features derived from free speech may be sufficient to detect fatigue." Moreover, Lou et al. (2022)* made use of the VSURF package by Genuer et al. (2010), a stepwise performance-based variable selection approach that is based on RFs. Other researchers did not mention a specific procedure but described implementing a stepwise backward algorithm for an RF in order to obtain a reduced set of features associated with the model's outcome. There were also statistical tests that, for example, identified brain regions with voxel-by-voxel two-sample t-tests (Lin et al., 2022)*, or the most informative unigrams (i.e., single words in speech data) using a chi-squared test for observed and expected frequencies (Wiegersma et al., 2022)*. Another example is Baurley et al. (2022)* who applied a Bayesian mixed effects SVM model that "provides both point estimates (estimated posterior means) and 95% equitailed credible intervals; with the interpretation that a variable is associated with heavy drinking if the 95% credible interval excludes zero." Finally, others used visual representations, such as saliency maps, heatmaps of, for example, (brain) images indicating which features (e.g., voxels or simply pixels of an image) contribute most to the model's outcome.

To identify eligible journals, we used the Journal Citation Reports Data from the Web of Science Core Collection(Clarivate, 2025) and only took into account journals with a 2022 journal impact factor of at least 1.0.

The smaller number of articles from 2024/2025 may partly reflect database indexing. Journals are added to the coverage of APA PsycInfo over time and their articles are indexed retrospectively, so some articles published in 2024/2025 had not yet been indexed at the time of our search. A shift in terminology may also contribute (see Limitations).

Note that we have defined "interpreting an effect" very strictly, and it extends beyond variable selection. For instance, this describes the shape or functional form of the relationship between a feature and the outcome, as well as the strength of the effect, which indicates how much the predicted outcome changes with varying values of a feature.
